name: Treaty with the Omaha, 1865
promises: Article 1: the Omaha ceded the northern part of their reservation; Royce records it was for locating the Winnebago (Royce p. 834).
Article 2: the United States to pay $50,000 on ratification, spent by the agent on goods, provisions, stock, buildings, tools and improvements on the reservation.
Article 3: Article 8 of the 1854 treaty extended for ten years, and $7,000 paid for damage from the Winnebago's temporary stay and timber use on Omaha land.
Article 4: the remaining reservation to be allotted in severalty, and whites not to go or reside on it.

breaches.what: The Omaha claimed fair compensation for the land ceded in 1865 for the Winnebago (Docket 225-B). The claim was never tried; it was settled together with the tribe's other claims in Docket 225 Consolidated by a compromise the Commission approved.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Omaha Tribe of Nebraska v. United States, Docket 225-B, settled in Docket 225 Consolidated (February 11, 1960)

source.title: Omaha Tribe of Nebraska et al. v. United States, Dockets 225-A to 225-D, Findings of Fact on Proposed Compromise Settlement (February 11, 1960), 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 392
source.publisher: Indian Claims Commission, via Oklahoma State University Library

compensation: The treaty price was $50,000 (Article 2) plus $7,000 in damages (Article 3). The Commission's summary of Docket 225-B gives the consideration as cash and provisions; the scanned figures are partly unreadable and are left out.
today: The Docket 225-B claim was settled, not decided, as part of the 1960 Docket 225 Consolidated compromise.

openQuestions: The settlement total for Docket 225 Consolidated and the acreage in Docket 225-B are poorly scanned; neither is recorded.
Royce (p. 837) records 20 more sections bought from the Omaha by Act of June 22, 1874 for the Winnebago; that is a separate event.
The Omaha Tribe's own account of the 1865 cession was not located in this pass.

plain.promised: The Omaha sold the northern part of their reservation, for the Winnebago, for $50,000 in goods and improvements and $7,000 in damages, and kept the rest as allotted land closed to whites.
plain.happened: The Omaha later claimed before the Indian Claims Commission that they were not fairly paid for this land. The claim was never decided.
plain.today: It was settled in 1960 as part of a compromise of all the tribe's claims in that case.
